subQuestions.questionText:
BUDGETS — SINDI'S BOUTIQUE

Sindi's Boutique sells up-market, luxury clothing. Sales have been on a downward spiral since March 2020 due to the economic decline.

Projected Income Statement for January 2022:
• Sales: R343 900
• Cost of sales: (R181 000)
• Gross profit: R162 900
• Operating expenses: (R190 220) — Employee costs R55 020; Rent expense R62 700; Electricity R50 000; Bad debts R13 900; Other R8 600
• Operating profit: (R27 320)
• Interest expense: (R13 350)
• Net profit (loss) for the month: (R40 670)

The Projected Income Statement is used by management for planning. Study it and explain whether Sindi's Boutique's plan is a successful one or not.
subQuestions.memoText:
Sindi's Boutique has planned to make a LOSS of R40 670 for January 2022. ✓ This is NOT a successful plan. ✓

Teaching point: A projected (budgeted) income statement is a plan; if the plan itself shows a loss, management is planning to go backwards and must change the plan before the period starts.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Interpreting a projected income statement

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.1. Describe what will ultimately happen to Sindi's Boutique if they keep on the path that they are on.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓✓:
• They will become insolvent (liabilities will exceed assets).
• They will have to close down.
• The capital / owner's equity will be eroded.

Teaching point: Sustained monthly losses erode owner's equity; once liabilities exceed assets the business is technically insolvent and cannot continue.

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.1. The sales have reduced significantly since lockdown. Explain in detail ONE factor that could have contributed to this.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE factor, explained (2 marks) ✓✓:
• The economic decline means people have less disposable income, so they cut down on luxuries like expensive clothing.
• Lower demand because there are fewer social gatherings (weddings, functions) at which to wear up-market clothing.
• Customers are afraid to go shopping in person because of the virus.

Teaching point: For a 'luxury' retailer, sales are highly sensitive to disposable income and to the social occasions that drive demand — both fell sharply during lockdown.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Explaining a decline in sales

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.1. Looking at the Projected Income Statement, name TWO strategies Sindi could implement to help make her business profitable again.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid strategies ✓✓:
• Change the product range to include different / cheaper clothing that more customers can afford.
• Cut expenses, e.g. move to premises that charge less rent.
• Control debtors better (stricter credit checks) to reduce the R13 900 bad debts.
• Advertise to the target market (magazines read by wealthy women or about weddings and matric dances).
• Use electricity-saving lighting and switch off after hours to reduce the R50 000 electricity cost.
• Pay off the loan to reduce the R13 350 interest expense.

Teaching point: Turnaround strategies either raise gross profit (product mix, mark-up, marketing) or cut costs (rent, electricity, bad debts, interest).

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1, plus:
• 80% of sales are on credit. Projected debtors collection: 5% in the month after the sale; 10% two months after; 60% three months after; 20% in the fourth month after; 5% written off at the end of the fourth month.
• Total sales: October R347 500; November R370 500; December R452 500; January R343 900 (from the projected income statement). Credit sales are 80% of total sales: October R278 000; November R296 400; December R362 000; January R275 120.

Complete the Debtors Collection Schedule for February 2022.
subQuestions.memoText:
DEBTORS COLLECTION SCHEDULE FOR FEBRUARY 2022:

          | Credit sales | February collection
October   | R278 000     | 278 000 × 5% = R13 900 ✓ (4 months after)
November  | R296 400     | 296 400 × 60% = R177 840 ✓ (3 months after)
December  | R362 000     | 362 000 × 10% = R36 200 ✓ (2 months after)
January   | R275 120     | 275 120 × 5% = R13 756 ✓ (1 month after)
Total cash from debtors in February: DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: Each month's credit sales are collected over the following four months in the given percentages; the February column picks the correct percentage for each prior month according to how many months have passed.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1 and 1.5, plus:
2. A fixed level of inventory is maintained.
3. Mark-up increases from 90% to 110% on 1 February 2022.
4. The premises owner will take dresses with a selling price of R13 650 (cost R6 500) in February; the selling price is deducted from February's rent.
5. 60% of stock purchases are for cash, 40% on credit.
6. Employee costs = gross salaries + 1% UIF + 10% pension + 20% medical aid. Sindi stops the pension and medical aid contributions from the end of January 2022.
7. Other expenses for February: cash purchases of consumables R4 000; depreciation on equipment R3 490; cash purchases of stationery R1 110.
8. One of three cash registers is sold for cash in February: cost R7 000; accumulated depreciation on date of sale R4 230; profit on sale R120.
9. Interest expense = interest on overdraft R3 945 + interest on loan R9 405 (capitalised to the loan monthly). A debit order of R23 000 pays off the loan every month.
• Cash sales for February = R53 004; payments to creditors = R74 100; bank balance at the beginning of February = (R200 325) overdrawn.

Complete the Cash Budget for February 2022, showing the calculation next to each item.
subQuestions.memoText:
CASH BUDGET FOR FEBRUARY 2022:

RECEIPTS (do not total):
• Cash sales: R53 004 ✓
• Cash from debtors: DO NOT CALCULATE (from 1.5)
• Asset disposal: 7 000 − 4 230 + 120 (profit) = R2 890 ✓

PAYMENTS (do not total):
• Cash purchases of stock: cost of sales for Feb = 53 004 × 100/20 × 100/210 = 126 200; + 6 500 (dresses to landlord at cost) = 132 700; × 60% cash = R79 620 ✓✓
  (mark-up now 110%, so cost of sales = selling price × 100/210; only 60% of purchases are paid in cash)
• Payments to creditors: R74 100 ✓
• Employee costs: 55 020 × 101/131 = R42 420 ✓ (remove the 10% pension and 20% medical aid, keep the 1% UIF, so 131% → 101%)
• Rent expense: 62 700 − 13 650 (dresses taken in lieu of rent) = R49 050 ✓
• Electricity: R50 000 ✓
• Other: 4 000 (consumables) + 1 110 (stationery) = R5 110 ✓ (depreciation R3 490 is non-cash, excluded)
• Loan repayment: R23 000 ✓
• Interest on overdraft: R3 945 ✓ (interest on loan R9 405 is capitalised, non-cash)

Cash deficit for the month: (R30 495)
Bank balance at the beginning of the month: (R200 325)
Bank balance at the end of the month: (R230 820)

Teaching point: A cash budget records only actual cash movements — depreciation and capitalised loan interest are excluded; goods taken by the landlord in lieu of rent both reduce the rent payment and (at cost) increase the stock that must be purchased.

subQuestions.questionText: What does the solvency ratio of a business measure?
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid answer ✓✓:
• The solvency ratio tests the risk of the business becoming insolvent / bankrupt.
• It tests the ability of the business to pay ALL its liabilities with ALL its assets.

Teaching point: Solvency (total assets : total liabilities) is a long-term measure of whether the business owns enough in total to cover everything it owes; below 1 : 1 the business is insolvent.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.6.

Estimated balances on 28 February 2022: Total assets R1 245 776; Non-current liabilities (loans) R1 254 000; Trade creditors R72 400. The bank balance at the end of February is an overdraft of R230 820 (from 1.6).

Calculate the expected solvency ratio of Sindi's Boutique on 28 February 2022.
subQuestions.memoText:
Solvency ratio = total assets : total liabilities
= 1 245 776 : (1 254 000 + 72 400 + 230 820)
= 1 245 776 : 1 557 220 ✓
= 0,8 : 1 ✓

Teaching point: Total liabilities includes the bank overdraft (a current liability). A solvency ratio below 1 : 1 means the business owes more than it owns — it is insolvent.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1. Sindi is considering closing Sindi's Boutique down and filing for bankruptcy (insolvency) — the courts would sell all her assets, business and personal, to pay her debts. She is considering starting a new online shop afterwards.

Discuss ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of (a) keeping her shop open, or (b) declaring bankruptcy, closing down and going online. Then advise Sindi on what she should do and explain the main reason for your advice. (The advantage of keeping the shop open may not be the same reason given for the disadvantage of closing down — do not repeat reasons.)
subQuestions.memoText:
KEEPING THE SHOP OPEN:
Advantage (✓): She will not lose her private assets by declaring bankruptcy; OR she already has customers and a reputation and can adapt what she has rather than start from scratch.
Disadvantage (✓): High, unmanageable overhead costs will lead to worse debt and interest; OR she is deeply in debt and, if she cannot change, will only lose more personal assets.

CLOSING DOWN, DECLARING BANKRUPTCY AND GOING ONLINE:
Advantage (✓): The court will write off her debt so it no longer hangs over her; OR online trading has low costs, can be run from home and should become profitable quickly; OR her debt stops growing; OR more people are shopping online.
Disadvantage (✓): She will have to build customers and a reputation from scratch; OR learn to market online; OR find new suppliers and a new market; OR she will lose her private assets; OR start-up costs of web design and marketing.

Advice and explanation (✓✓): Any advice that makes sense, with a clear main reason (e.g. 'Close down and go online, because her current cost structure — rent, electricity, interest — can never be profitable at these sales levels, whereas an online model removes most of those costs').

Teaching point: A sound recommendation weighs the protection of personal assets and existing goodwill against the burden of a cost structure the business can no longer support.

questions.title: Company Analysis (Dis-Chem Ltd vs Clicks Ltd)

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY ANALYSIS — DIS-CHEM LTD vs CLICKS LTD (both listed pharmaceutical retailers)

Profitability ratios on 31 August:
                              | Dis-Chem 2020 | Dis-Chem 2019 | Clicks 2020 | Clicks 2019
Gross profit on sales          |        22,95% |        24,38% |      20,98% |      21,34%
Total income on sales          |        28,67% |         29,1% |      27,28% |      27,59%
Operating expenses on sales    |         23,6% |        22,68% |      19,23% |      19,51%
Operating profit on sales      |         5,08% |         6,42% |       7,34% |       7,94%
Net profit after tax on sales  |          2,5% |          3,5% |        5,5% |       5,37%

Both companies earn income from advertising on behalf of other companies, recorded in 'Other Income'. Explain, by doing a calculation, which company was the most effective in earning other income in 2020.
subQuestions.memoText:
Difference between total income on sales and gross profit on sales (this gap is 'other income' as a % of sales):
Dis-Chem: 28,67 − 22,95 = 5,72% ✓✓
Clicks: 27,28 − 20,98 = 6,30% ✓✓
OR as a % of gross profit: Dis-Chem (5,72 ÷ 22,95) × 100 = 24,92%; Clicks (6,30 ÷ 20,98) × 100 = 30,03%.

CLICKS was more effective ✓ — it has the bigger difference between gross profit and total income, i.e. it earns proportionally more other income.

Teaching point: 'Total income on sales' minus 'gross profit on sales' isolates the non-trading income (like advertising commission) as a percentage of sales; the higher gap shows the more effective earner of that income.

subQuestions.questionText: Use the profitability ratios in 2.1.1. Analyse which company was more profitable in 2020. Substantiate your answer with FOUR points.
subQuestions.memoText:
CLICKS was more profitable. Any FOUR points ✓✓✓✓:
• Although its mark-up (gross profit %) was lower, Clicks earned proportionally more other income.
• Clicks controlled its expenses better — operating expenses on sales fell slightly, while Dis-Chem's rose (22,68% → 23,6%).
• Clicks's operating expenses on sales were far lower: 19,23% vs Dis-Chem's 23,6%.
• Clicks's operating profit on sales was higher by 2,26% (7,34% vs 5,08%).
• Clicks's net profit after tax on sales was higher by 2,82% (5,5% vs 2,5%).
• Dis-Chem's financing cost percentage was higher (bigger drop from operating profit to net profit).
• Clicks's net profit improved year on year, while Dis-Chem's decreased.
• Clicks's net profit is roughly three times that of Dis-Chem.

Teaching point: 'More profitable' is judged on the bottom line relative to sales (net profit on sales) and on the trend, not on gross mark-up alone.

subQuestions.questionText: Most companies' profitability dropped significantly during 2020. Explain the probable reason why Clicks's profitability INCREASED during this time.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid reason ✓✓:
• As a pharmacy, Clicks could keep trading through lockdown when most other retailers had to close.
• People bought large volumes of health products, sanitisers, vitamins and medicines to stay healthy through the pandemic.

Teaching point: 'Essential service' status during lockdown gave pharmacy retailers both continued trading and a surge in demand for health-related products.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Pandemic effect on a pharmacy retailer

subQuestions.questionText:
DIS-CHEM figures for 2020 (R'000): Sales R24 944 000; Cost of sales R19 219 000; Inventories R4 840 424 (2020) and R4 339 208 (2019).

Calculate the number of days' stock on hand for Dis-Chem for 2020 (use the average inventory).
subQuestions.memoText:
Days' stock on hand (Dis-Chem 2020):
= [(4 840 424 + 4 339 208) ÷ 2] ÷ 19 219 000 × 365
= 4 589 816 ÷ 19 219 000 × 365
= 87,17 days ✓✓✓

Teaching point: Days' stock on hand = average inventory ÷ cost of sales × 365. Using the average (opening + closing ÷ 2) smooths out a large change in the stock level during the year.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Days' stock on hand

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 2.2.1. Explain how selling health foods would impact Dis-Chem's number of days' stock on hand. Will it make the period longer or shorter, and why?
subQuestions.memoText:
It will SHORTEN the period ✓. Food has a shorter shelf life than the other products Dis-Chem sells (toiletries, appliances), so it must be sold quickly — probably within three months — which pulls the average holding period down. ✓

Teaching point: Perishable lines force faster stock turnover; adding them to the product mix lowers the overall days-on-hand figure.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Effect of product mix on stock turnover

subQuestions.questionText:
CLICKS ratios on 31 August:
                              | 2020        | 2019
Current ratio                  |     1,2 : 1 |     1,2 : 1
Acid test ratio                |    0,59 : 1 |    0,62 : 1
Days of stock on hand          |     66 days |     70 days
Debtors collection period      |     31 days |     37 days
Creditors payment period       |     60 days |     73 days
Cash & cash equivalents (R'000)|   2 152 483 |   2 613 554

Summarise Clicks's liquidity by writing down THREE detailed points, and write a conclusion stating whether they will be able to pay off their current debts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE detailed points ✓✓✓✓ (2 marks each up to the cap, then conclusion):
• Current ratio 1,2 : 1 and acid test 0,59 : 1 — about half of the current assets is stock, which is a reasonable balance for a retailer.
• Stock turnover improved by 4 days (70 → 66), a good rate for their products.
• Trade and other receivables are being collected 6 days faster (37 → 31 days).
• Clicks holds high cash reserves — strong, immediately available liquidity.
• The creditors payment period dropped by 13 days (73 → 60) — technically worse for liquidity, but Clicks has the cash and chooses to pay suppliers sooner.
• The current ratio held constant at 1,2 : 1; the acid test slipped slightly (0,62 → 0,59) but is still about half the current ratio, showing assets and liabilities are in balance.

Conclusion ✓✓: Clicks WILL be able to pay off its current debts (strong cash position, fast-improving collection and stock turnover).

Teaching point: Liquidity analysis reads the current and acid-test ratios together with the turnover periods (stock, debtors, creditors) and the cash balance — a ratio slightly below the 2:1 rule of thumb is fine when turnover is fast and cash is abundant.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Liquidity analysis and conclusion

subQuestions.questionText: Dis-Chem's goal is to expand by 18 new stores per year, expected to cost R370 million next financial year. List TWO disadvantages for Dis-Chem should they issue more shares to finance this expansion.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO disadvantages ✓✓:
• Issuing more shares dilutes ROCE, ROSHE (ROSE) and EPS.
• If dividends are paid, they will cost more in total (more shares in issue).
• Existing shareholders' percentage of control is diluted — they may be unhappy and sell.
• The market value of the shares may be diluted.

Teaching point: A share issue spreads the same profit over more shares, weakening per-share and return ratios, and dilutes both control and (potentially) share price.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Disadvantages of a share issue

subQuestions.questionText:
Dis-Chem 2020 figures (R'000): Non-current liabilities R3 075 932; Equity R2 620 371; existing debt-equity ratio for 2019 was 1,5 : 1.

Calculate what the new debt-equity ratio would be should Dis-Chem increase their loan by R370 million (R370 000 thousand).
subQuestions.memoText:
New debt-equity ratio:
= (3 075 932 + 370 000) : 2 620 371
= 3 445 932 : 2 620 371 ✓✓
= 1,32 : 1 ✓

Teaching point: Debt-equity ratio = non-current liabilities : ordinary shareholders' equity. Adding R370 million of loan raises the numerator only, pushing the ratio up (more financial risk / gearing).

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 2.3.1 and 2.3.2. Dis-Chem's return on total capital employed is 12% and the effective interest rate on non-current liabilities is 4,5%. Dis-Chem already has bank overdrafts.

Discuss whether Dis-Chem should finance the new stores by increasing their loan or by issuing more shares. Discuss THREE points.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE points ✓✓✓ (arguments either way are accepted if valid):

Loan:
• The debt-equity ratio shows relatively high risk, BUT Dis-Chem is positively geared — the 12% return on capital employed is well above the 4,5% interest rate.
• Interest on the loan is tax-deductible, reducing profit and the tax expense; dividends on shares are not.
• A loan can be repaid and the interest expense removed later; shares are permanent and carry an ongoing dividend expectation.
• Do NOT dilute EPS, ROCE, ROSHE.

New shares:
• Dis-Chem already has bank overdrafts, so avoiding more interest would help liquidity.
• Shares do not have to be repaid; a loan does.
• Dividends are discretionary; loan interest is compulsory.
• The bank may refuse further lending because Dis-Chem is already highly geared.

Teaching point: The gearing decision weighs positive gearing and the tax shield on interest against the liquidity strain of compulsory repayments and the dilution caused by a share issue.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Loan vs share issue

subQuestions.questionText:
DIS-CHEM: Equity on 31 August 2020 = R2 620 371 thousand; total issued shares = 860 085 000.

Calculate the Net Asset Value (NAV) per share for Dis-Chem for 2020.
subQuestions.memoText:
Net Asset Value per share (Dis-Chem 2020):
= 2 620 371 000 ÷ 860 085 000
= R3,05 = 304,67 cents ≈ 305 cents per share ✓✓✓

Teaching point: NAV per share = ordinary shareholders' equity ÷ number of issued shares. It shows the book value backing each share, useful to compare against the market price.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Net Asset Value per share

subQuestions.questionText:
DIS-CHEM share price on the JSE: 2 225 cents (31 Aug 2019); 1 826 cents (31 Aug 2020). Earnings per share rose from 65 cents to 75 cents; dividend per share fell from 33 cents to 16 cents (no dividend declared on 31 Aug 2020 due to cash-flow concerns).

Dis-Chem's share value nearly doubled when it listed at the end of 2016 but has been dropping ever since. Explain a likely reason why the share price has been dropping.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid reason ✓✓:
• The company has not performed up to investors' expectations since listing, so disappointed investors have been selling their shares.
• Falling profits and reduced / no dividends since 2019 make the share less attractive, so investors sell and the price falls.

Teaching point: A share price reflects market sentiment about future returns — weak profit growth and dividend cuts drive sellers into the market and push the price down.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Explaining a falling share price

subQuestions.questionText:
Earnings per share: Dis-Chem 75 cents; Clicks 751 cents. Issued shares: Dis-Chem 860 085 000; Clicks 250 212 000.

List TWO reasons why Clicks's EPS is much bigger than Dis-Chem's.
subQuestions.memoText:
Two reasons ✓✓:
• Clicks had a much better net profit (R1 880 175 thousand vs R623 600 thousand).
• Clicks issued far fewer shares (250 million vs 860 million), so the profit is divided among fewer shares.

Teaching point: EPS = earnings ÷ number of shares — a company can have a high EPS through higher earnings, fewer shares, or both.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Earnings per share comparison

subQuestions.questionText: Dis-Chem decided not to declare a final dividend on 31 August 2020 to preserve cash flow. Explain ONE point that SUPPORTS this decision.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE point ✓✓:
• Dis-Chem already has a bank overdraft, so cash should be conserved rather than paid out.
• The future financial impact of the coronavirus is uncertain, so it is prudent to keep a cash buffer.

Teaching point: Retaining profit instead of paying dividends is defensible when the company is already borrowing short-term and faces an uncertain trading outlook.

subQuestions.questionText: Use all the Dis-Chem and Clicks information above. If you had R10 000 to spend on either Dis-Chem shares OR Clicks shares, which would you buy? Discuss THREE factors that led you to this decision.
subQuestions.memoText:
Either choice is accepted with THREE valid supporting factors ✓✓✓:

Clicks:
• Better profitability (net profit on sales 5,5% vs 2,5%).
• Better and improving returns — ROSHE 37,8%, ROTCE 25%, rising EPS.
• Dividends per share increased (450 cents); better dividend-to-earnings ratio.
• Better liquidity and rising market share price and NAV.
• Established, with a long track record on the JSE.

Dis-Chem:
• More growth potential (younger company, aggressive store roll-out).
• The shares offer better value for money (lower price relative to NAV).
• Returns, though below Clicks's, are still good and have room to improve.
• Net asset value increased by a higher percentage than Clicks's.

Teaching point: A share-selection argument must be internally consistent — pick the company and then cite profitability, returns, dividends, liquidity and growth evidence that all point the same way.

subQuestions.questionText: Dis-Chem was found guilty of excessive face-mask pricing — in late February 2020 it raised mask prices by between 43% and 261%. Discuss how the King Code should have influenced Dis-Chem's decision to increase the price of face masks by such a large amount.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid point ✓:
• The King Code deals with corporate governance (ethical behaviour), so Dis-Chem should have been guided by what was ethical rather than only by profit.
• The King Code also requires a company to be socially accountable — Dis-Chem should have considered the impact of the price hike on the community during a pandemic.

Teaching point: The King Code sets the expectation that directors act ethically and account for the social impact of business decisions, not just the financial return.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - King Code and ethics

subQuestions.questionText:
Dis-Chem was fined R1,2 million by the Competition Tribunal. The Competition Commission originally wanted to fine them 10% of their sales.

Do you think it would have been ethically correct for the Competition Tribunal to fine Dis-Chem 10% of their sales? Explain your reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Either view is accepted with a valid reason ✓:

No:
• Masks are only one of very many products, so mask sales are a tiny fraction of total sales — 10% of ALL sales is disproportionate.
• A fine of nearly R2,5 billion would push Dis-Chem into a roughly R2,4 billion loss and risk insolvency, harming the shareholders who own the company.

Yes:
• Exploiting people during a pandemic is ethically wrong and deserves a heavy penalty.
• The standard legal practice is that the fine should be 10% of total sales.

Teaching point: Proportionality is central to a fair penalty — the fine should reflect the wrongdoing without destroying an otherwise viable company.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Ethics of a competition fine

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 2.7.1. Discuss the financial impact on Dis-Chem had their fine been 10% of their sales. Explain how this would have affected their Statement of Financial Position (Balance Sheet).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid point ✓:
• Dis-Chem would not have had the cash to pay the fine, so current liabilities (and possibly non-current liabilities, if a loan were needed) would have risen sharply.
• The resulting net loss (about R2,4 billion) would have wiped out retained earnings almost completely, reducing equity.

Teaching point: A fine that exceeds available cash forces new borrowing (liabilities up) and, through the loss, erodes retained earnings (equity down) — the balance sheet weakens on both sides.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Balance sheet impact of a large fine

subQuestions.questionText:
RECONCILIATIONS — FUN FITNESS

Jay owns a gym, Fun Fitness, which buys all its equipment from Muscle Machines (its only creditor). Statement received from Muscle Machines on 30 November 2021:

Date       | Transaction        | Debit    | Credit  | Balance
2021 Aug 8 | Invoice X23        | 88 000   |         | 88 000
Sept 5     | Invoice X27        | 74 800   |         | 162 800
Sept 7     | Credit note N73    |          | 12 200  | 150 600
Oct 1      | Interest           | 4 400    |         | 155 000
Oct 19     | Invoice X32        | 120 000  |         | 275 000
Oct 29     | EFT                |          | 81 840  | 193 160
Oct 29     | Discount           |          | 6 160   | 187 000
Nov 1      | Interest           | 3 730    |         | 190 730

Terms: discount granted on payments made within 30 days of statement; 5% per month interest charged after 30 days overdue.

Fill in the age analysis as it would appear at the bottom of the statement (columns: 90 Days | 60 Days | 30 Days | Current). Ignore all errors and omissions and use ONLY the figures given in the statement. Show all the figures that go into each block (you do not need to total each block).
subQuestions.memoText:
AGE ANALYSIS (using statement figures only):

90 Days (August): 88 000 − 88 000 (allocated by the Oct EFT/discount) ✓
60 Days (September): 74 800 − 12 200 (credit note N73) ✓
30 Days (October): 4 400 (interest) + 120 000 (Invoice X32) ✓
Current (November): 3 730 (interest) ✓

Teaching point: An age analysis buckets the outstanding balance by how long each item has been owed. The oldest debt is cleared first by any payment, so the August invoice and part of September are settled by the October EFT and discount.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 3.1. Fun Fitness receives a 12% trade discount from Muscle Machines but must pay within 30 days of statement or be charged 5% per month interest. Other suppliers of the same equipment offer only a 3% trade discount but allow payment within 90 days.

Jay decided to keep Muscle Machines as his supplier even though Fun Fitness does not always have the cash flow to pay within 30 days of statement. Analyse whether Jay made the correct decision. Use figures or calculations in your analysis.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks: 1 for mentioning the trade discount OR the interest only (not linked); 2 for mentioning both the trade discount AND the interest and linking them; 3 for a valid linked conclusion ✓✓✓.

• Fun Fitness gets a 12% trade discount but pays a 5% per month interest penalty if late.
• If they pay after 90 days (3 months late-ish), interest of roughly 10% would leave a net benefit of only about 2% — worse than the 3% trade discount from the other suppliers, so at 90 days they should switch suppliers.
• If they can pay within about 60 days, the net benefit is roughly 7%, which beats the other suppliers' 3%, so staying with Muscle Machines is correct.
• Conclusion: Jay's decision is correct ONLY if Fun Fitness can usually pay within about 60 days; if payment routinely stretches to 90 days, he should move to a 3%-discount / 90-day supplier.

Teaching point: Compare the net cost of trade credit — trade discount earned MINUS interest penalty suffered — against the alternative supplier's terms; the better deal depends on how quickly you actually pay.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 3.1, plus:
• Muscle Machines balance at year-end 30 November 2020: R133 150.
• Muscle Machines balance at year-end 30 November 2021: R152 760.
• Total credit purchases from Muscle Machines for the year: R790 800.
• Total returns to Muscle Machines for the year: R80 700.

Calculate the average number of days that Fun Fitness is taking to pay Muscle Machines.
subQuestions.memoText:
Creditors payment period:
Average creditors = (133 150 + 152 760) ÷ 2 = R142 955 ✓
Net credit purchases = 790 800 − 80 700 = R710 100 ✓
Days = 142 955 ÷ 710 100 × 365 = 73,48 days ≈ 74 days ✓✓

Teaching point: Creditors payment period = average creditors ÷ net credit purchases × 365. At ~74 days Fun Fitness is well beyond Muscle Machines' 30-day terms — hence the interest penalties.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 3.1. On 29 October Muscle Machines received an EFT of R81 840 from Fun Fitness and then granted a discount of R6 160 (shown on the statement).

Calculate the percentage discount Muscle Machines gave Fun Fitness when they paid, and comment on whether it was a financially sound decision for Muscle Machines to grant Fun Fitness that discount.
subQuestions.memoText:
Percentage discount = 6 160 ÷ (81 840 + 6 160) = 6 160 ÷ 88 000 = 7% ✓

Comment ✓✓:
• Muscle Machines should NOT have granted the discount, because Fun Fitness did not pay within the 30 days stipulated in the terms.
• The 7% discount is more than the interest Muscle Machines was charging on that same debt, so Muscle Machines ends up about 2% worse off even though Fun Fitness paid late.

Teaching point: A settlement discount is only worthwhile to the supplier if it is smaller than the finance cost saved by getting paid earlier — and it should not be given at all when the customer breaches the payment terms.

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 3.1. Errors and omissions found when comparing the Creditors Statement to the Creditors Ledger:
1. Muscle Machines forgot the 12% trade discount on invoice X32 (R120 000). Fun Fitness recorded the invoice with the trade discount subtracted.
2. Invoice X77 for R24 000 in the Creditors Ledger account was actually from Fitness Magazine for advertisements.
3. Fun Fitness was not aware of the discount Muscle Machines granted on 29 October (R6 160).
4. Fun Fitness paid Muscle Machines R50 000 via EFT on 30 November, entered in the CPJ and posted to the ledgers.
5. Muscle Machines incorrectly calculated the interest on 1 November; the correct interest was R3 130. The 1 November interest had not been entered in Fun Fitness's Creditors Ledger at all.

Statement balance (incorrect): R190 730. Creditors Ledger balance (incorrect): R152 760.

Reconcile the statement to the ledger: show the amounts that go into the Creditors Reconciliation Statement and the amounts that go into the Creditors Ledger account.
subQuestions.memoText:
CREDITORS RECONCILIATION — 30 November 2021:

                                   | Reconciliation Statement | Creditors Ledger
Incorrect balance                  | 190 730                  | 152 760
1. Trade discount (12% × 120 000)  | (14 400) ✓               |
2. Invoice X77 (Fitness Magazine)  |                          | (24 000) ✓
3. Discount received 29 Oct        | + 6 160 (or) ✓           | (6 160) ✓
4. EFT paid 30 Nov                 | (50 000) ✓              |
5. Interest 1 Nov (3 730 − 3 130 = 600 overstated on statement; R3 130 to be entered in ledger) | (600) ✓ | 3 130 ✓
Corrected balance                  | DO NOT CALCULATE         | DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: Errors made by the supplier are fixed on the Reconciliation Statement side; errors and omissions in the business's own books are fixed in the Creditors Ledger account. Both columns must end on the same corrected balance.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the main difference between the work an internal auditor does and the work an external auditor does.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓:
• An internal auditor examines the company's processes and procedures (internal controls) on an ongoing basis.
• An external auditor verifies that the annual financial statements are a fair reflection of the company's finances, giving shareholders assurance that the information can be relied upon.

Teaching point: Internal audit is about how the business runs (controls, efficiency); external audit is an independent opinion on whether the published financial statements are fairly presented.

subQuestions.questionText: External auditors are supposed to offer an unbiased audit. Explain what this means.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓:
• They must have no connection to the company they are auditing — an outsider's opinion, because they are not part of the company.
• Examples that show independence: not allowed to own shares in that company; not allowed to have family who work there; not allowed to accept gifts; not allowed to socialise with the directors or managers.

Teaching point: 'Unbiased' (independent) means nothing about the auditor's personal or financial situation could influence the audit opinion.

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss TWO processes an internal auditor should look at when auditing creditors.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO ✓✓:
• The process of drawing up the creditors reconciliation each month.
• The process of entering source documents (invoices, debit notes, EFTs) into the journals (CJ, CAJ, CPJ).
• The process of posting those journals to the ledger accounts.
• Whether creditors are being paid within their agreed terms.
• The procurement process — how suppliers are selected.

Teaching point: Auditing creditors means testing the full cycle — source document, journal, ledger, reconciliation, payment — plus the controls around choosing suppliers.
